extracted.intended_audience: researchers and practitioners in humor research, psycholinguistics, cognitive psychology, NLP/machine learning using lexical norms
extracted.subtask_description: Collecting and reporting crowd-sourced humor ratings for individual English words (single-word level), including methods for stimulus selection, rating procedure, data cleaning, reliability, and demographic analyses. The dataset is intended for researchers who need word-level humor norms or wish to relate humor to other lexical metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humor rating scale
rubrics_metrics.description: Participants rated words on a scale from 1 (humorless = not funny at all) to 5 (humorous = most funny), with 3 as neutral.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extremes labeled: 1 = 'humorless' and 5 = 'humorous'. The 5-point scale allows intermediates; participants were instructed to select 3 if the word is neutral (neither humorous nor humorless).

rubrics_metrics.name: Instruction to use first immediate reaction
rubrics_metrics.description: Participants were told to work at a rapid pace and not spend too much time thinking about each word, making ratings based on their first and immediate reaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The introduction explicitly requests rapid responses to capture intuitive humor appraisal rather than deliberative judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calibrator words and ordering
rubrics_metrics.description: A set of 11 calibrator words spanning the humor range (from pilot study) were presented to all participants before the random words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Calibrators shown first to illustrate the range of the humor scale and increase reliability of subsequent ratings; calibrators were rated by all 821 participants and their distributions were reported individually.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stimulus selection from intersecting lexical norms
rubrics_metrics.description: Word list was drawn from the intersection of several existing norms (valence/arousal/dominance, age of acquisition, lexical decision, and frequency), yielding 7,775 words, from which 5,000 were randomly sampled for the pool.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This selection allows linking humor ratings to many existing lexical metrics and ensures overlap with prior normative datasets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Per-participant stimulus presentation (211 words)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each participant rated 211 words: the 11 calibrator words followed by 200 randomly sampled words from the 5,000-word pool (sample different per participant).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The random sample was generated in real time when participant opened the questionnaire. After rating a word, it disappeared from the list; participants pressed 'Submit' when finished and were debriefed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Participant recruitment and eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Participants were recruited via Amazon Mechanical Turk; any registered MTurk member could participate but had to fully complete the study and could do the study only once.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Language screening conducted (participants who indicated primary language not English were removed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Compensation and task duration
rubrics_metrics.description: Each participant was paid US$1; the study took approximately 15 minutes including instructions and debrief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Payment and expected time are reported as part of participant protocol/feasibility considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data trimming / exclusion criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Participants were removed for incomplete submissions, errors in the data, improper submissions (102 removed), low variability of responses (sd < 0.2; 5 removed), and indicating primary language not English (22 removed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Final dataset included 821 participants after these exclusions. Partial data were not recorded and only fully completed submissions were retained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimum and average number of raters per word
rubrics_metrics.description: Each of the 4,997 words was rated by at least 15 participants, with an average of approx. 33 raters per word (M = 32.93, SD = 5.64).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensures a baseline sample size per item for stable mean estimates; the 11 calibrators were rated by all participants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggregation into Mean Humor Rating (MHR)
rubrics_metrics.description: For each word, humor ratings were summed and divided by number of participants rating the word to compute the Mean Humor Rating (MHR).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MHR reported for all participants combined and computed separately by gender and by age-group splits; standard deviations and n are provided alongside means.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting per-demographic MHRs
rubrics_metrics.description: MHRs are provided separately for participants identifying as male and female, and for younger vs older age groups (median split at age 32).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dataset columns include mean_M/sd_M/n_M, mean_F/sd_F/n_F, mean_young/sd_young/n_young, and mean_old/sd_old/n_old to facilitate demographic analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Age-group construction (median split)
rubrics_metrics.description: Younger and older groups were constructed using a median split of participant ages (younger: age ≤ 32; older: age > 32).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Group sizes and descriptive statistics (means, SDs, min/max) were reported; authors note the median-split is an analytic choice and provide age-separated ratings for independent analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliability assessment (split-half)
rubrics_metrics.description: Split-half reliability of individual ratings was calculated and reported as 0.64.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This value is compared to previous norms (e.g., arousal ratings 0.69) and interpreted as indicating considerable individual differences; reliability justifies dataset use but indicates variability across raters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distributional analysis and reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: The distribution of MHRs across words was analyzed (positively skewed; range of 3.14 units), and extreme items were identified (most humorless and most humorous words).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors report skewness contrasted with valence norms, provide figures and tables of most extreme words, and discuss implications (majority rated closer to humorless).

rubrics_metrics.name: Gender and age difference analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors analyze and report correlations between male and female MHRs (r = .60) and list words with largest gender disagreements; similarly, list words with largest disagreements between younger and older groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors identify outliers by absolute differences and show agreement subsets (e.g., 5% lowest disagreement) and caution that some sampling criteria (like 5% threshold) are arbitrary and left for researchers to adjust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correlational analyses with existing lexical measures
rubrics_metrics.description: MHRs were correlated with 11 lexical measures from prior norms (e.g., frequency, reaction time, concreteness), with the strongest correlation found with frequency (less frequent words rated more humorous) and correlations with lexical decision reaction times.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Table of correlations provided; authors suggest these relationships can guide investigations of underlying mechanisms of humor and predictor models for machine learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analytic transparency and encouragement for re-use
rubrics_metrics.description: Complete dataset (mean and sd per group, n per group) is made freely available on GitHub as CSV; authors encourage readers to design and carry out their own analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dataset organized alphabetically by word; authors explicitly state arbitrary analytic choices (e.g., 5% subsampling) and recommend researchers perform more comprehensive analyses using the provided data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation mechanics and UI behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: On the online questionnaire each word had five buttons (1–5) under it, labeled at extremes; after selecting a rating the word disappeared from the list.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This UI design supports rapid single-response per item and avoids repeated ratings; participants submitted at the end and were debriefed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sampling strategy to increase rater exposure per word
rubrics_metrics.description: The initial 7,775-word intersection was randomly sampled down to 5,000 words to increase the number of raters exposed to a single word given a fixed number of participants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sampling reduction rationale: with fixed participant budget, smaller pool increases per-word rating counts and hence reliability of MHR estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality-control criterion for low-variance responders
rubrics_metrics.description: Respondents whose standard deviation of humor ratings across items was smaller than 0.2 were removed as indicating near-constant responding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This threshold identifies and excludes participants who chose roughly the same value for all words, guarding against inattentive or non-differentiating responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimum acceptable language background
rubrics_metrics.description: Participants who indicated their primary language was not English were excluded from the final dataset.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensures ratings reflect native/primary-English speakers' humor appraisals; 22 participants removed for this reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data fields and organization for public release
rubrics_metrics.description: Released CSV includes for each word: mean_ALL, sd_ALL, n_ALL, mean_M/sd_M/n_M, mean_F/sd_F/n_F, mean_young/sd_young/n_young, mean_old/sd_old/n_old.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sheet is organized alphabetically by word label to facilitate lookup; authors provide GitHub repository link for download and reuse.
